mechanisms: Evening light from LE-eBook phase delayed the circadian clock, delaying the nadir of the circadian rhythm of sleep propensity, resulting in an indirect effect on morning sleepiness.
Phase delay of the circadian clock is consistent with the slower rise in the rate of accumulation of REM sleep.
Change in the timing of REM sleep likely represents a delay in the circadian rhythm of REM sleep propensity.
Spectral composition of the light emitted by the LE-eBook (short-wavelength-enriched light) explains the magnitude of melatonin-suppressing and phase-shifting response.
Exposure to short-wavelength monochromatic light in the evening induces greater circadian and alerting responses.
limitations: Melatonin suppression was assessed only on the fifth and final evening of each reading condition.
The fixed 4-h duration of evening reading sessions may not capture all real-world variability of screen time exposure.
The LE-eBook was set to maximum brightness throughout the 4-h reading session, which may not reflect typical user behavior.

mechanisms: The short-wavelength-enriched light emitted by electronic devices produces alerting effects, suppresses the sleep-promoting hormone melatonin, and phase-shifts the biological clock to a later time.
The phase delay of the circadian clock, induced by evening light exposure, delays the nadir of the circadian rhythm of sleep propensity, leading to reduced alertness the following morning.

The spectral composition of the light from the LE-eBook, which is rich in short-wavelength light, induces a greater melatonin-suppressing and phase-shifting response than would be predicted by its photopic illuminance (lux) alone.
limitations: Melatonin suppression was assessed on the fifth and final evening of each reading condition, by which time a phase shift had likely already occurred (though this was controlled for in the analysis).
The duration of the evening reading sessions was 4 hours long, which may be longer than typical for some users, but is within the range of total screen time for many individuals.
The light-emitting eBook was set to maximum brightness throughout the reading session, which may not reflect typical use.

mechanisms: The vivid representation of interior colors in IVEs allows participants to understand color symbolism psychologically, leading to a precise perception of interior colors.
Overarousal from a color scheme (e.g., red) can deteriorate performance on complicated tasks that require significant attention, as suggested by the Yerkers-Dodson law.
Dizziness from using a Head-Mounted Display (HMD) might have reduced stimulation from color schemes, potentially explaining the overall decrease in heart rates across all conditions.
Insufficient exposure time in the IVE may prevent the full physiological response to arousing colors (e.g., red) from manifesting, unlike in studies with longer exposure in physical environments.
limitations: Wearing a Head-Mounted Display (HMD) can cause discomfort or dizziness, making IVEs unsuitable for long-duration studies.
Participants' awareness of being observed (Hawthorn effect) might have influenced their responses more than the colors themselves.
The use of highly saturated colors may not reflect real-world interior spaces, limiting the applicability of the findings.
The sample consisted mostly of local college students, which limits the generalizability of findings to other populations (e.g., older people, employees).
Some nearsighted participants perceived the IVE models as blurry, which could negatively affect their sense of presence and color perception.
The study only used three measures (emotion, heart rate, proofreading performance), so findings cannot be generalized to other indicators like environmental satisfaction or cognitive performance.
All participants were Asian, and color perception can vary by culture and geographical proximity.

mechanisms: Artists acquire different viewing strategies as a function of expertise in the apprehension of exact physical properties of scenes and objects, rather than general conceptual associations.
Structural features acquire meaningfulness for artists as cues for accurate rendition.
Artists become more skilled at extracting and remembering a greater variety of visual features because this is relevant to the production of pictures.
Scanning behaviour of artists is related to training in figurative rendition, which requires correctly apprehending exact physical features of picture elements.
Figurative rendition necessitates that the ability to apprehend exact physical properties of objects and scenes takes priority over preconceptions.
Production of figurative artwork involves enhanced attention to exact physical properties, suggesting training effects.
Artists' lower fMRI activation in facial processing suggests more efficient processing of facial information (from Solso 2001).
Kosslyn et al.'s (1989) distinction between categorical (general spatial properties) and coordinate (precise spatial locations) visual properties explains drawing skill development.
In figurative rendition, coordinate information becomes immediately important for accurate depiction.
Preconceptions of what a model 'is' can interfere with the ability to see what is actually there.
Priming for past experiences may hinder new episodic encoding by reducing encoding variability (Wagner et al. 2000).
limitations: The nature of the abstract pictures used (lacking striking focal areas and high contrast) may limit comparability with other studies (e.g., Zangemeister et al. 1995).
The absence of repetition effects in artists may indicate a radical deviation from normal viewing strategies, requiring further work to assess.
The study does not fully account for the role of motor aspects of drawing in laymen's difficulties in rendering natural scenes.

mechanisms: Artists' scanning behavior is related to training in figurative rendition, which requires the ability to correctly apprehend the exact physical features of picture elements.

Artists develop a processing strategy that prioritizes coordinate spatial relations (precise metric locations) over categorical spatial relations (general properties and proportions), which helps overcome preconceptions about objects.

The absence of repetition effects (fewer, longer fixations on second viewing) in artists may suggest a reduction in priming, leading to less encoding variability and allowing for the extraction and memory of a greater variety of visual features.
limitations: The nature of the picture stimuli (e.g., lack of striking focal areas in abstract pictures) may have influenced the results, potentially explaining less dramatic findings compared to previous studies.
The unexpected finding that artists do not demonstrate repetition effects in their eye movements is difficult to account for and requires further investigation.
The study's conclusions about the absence of repetition effects in artists are tentative, with the authors noting that 'Further work is needed to assess this finding'.
